title: Groundnut Soup with Kpakpo Shito
author: Zoe Adjei
desc: The same cook's other printing — eight green kpakpo shito instead of two scotch bonnets, half a litre of ready-made chalé sauce, and up to 200 g of peanut butter.
longDesc: The same author's groundnut soup appeared in a magazine profile in a noticeably different form, and the differences are worth having side by side. Two kilos of mixed bone-in chicken rather than two 850 g packs, five hundred millilitres of uncooked chalé sauce measured in rather than blended fresh, up to two hundred grams of peanut butter rather than a hundred and fifty, a full tablespoon of extra-hot chilli powder rather than half a teaspoon, and eight green kpakpo shito chillies where the other version uses one or two scotch bonnets. The method and the endpoint are identical.
ingredients: 500-750 ml water or good-quality chicken stock
8 green kpakpo shito chillies, or 1-2 scotch bonnet
steps: Simmer the chicken in the stock with the onion, ginger, garlic, chillies, chilli powder, curry powder, salt and pepper for 25 minutes, until the juices run clear, skimming the froth.
Stir in the 500 ml of uncooked chalé sauce.
Add the peanut butter gradually, letting each addition dissolve.
Drop in the pierced red scotch bonnet.
Cook 45 minutes to 1 hour on low, stirring regularly, until the peanut oil separates on top.
Check that the meat is falling from the bone and the consistency is soupy.
Garnish with the crushed peanuts and julienned spring onions.
chefTips: Eight kpakpo shito is a lot of chilli by volume but they are aromatic rather than brutal — this is the more fragrant of the two printings, not simply the hotter one.

A full tablespoon of extra-hot chilli powder, against half a teaspoon to a teaspoon in the other version. That is a sixfold difference from one cook, so taste as you go rather than trusting either figure blindly.
Five hundred millilitres of chalé sauce measured in, rather than blended fresh into the pot. If you keep chalé sauce in the fridge, this is the quicker route — see GHA031.
Up to 200 g of peanut butter makes a distinctly thicker soup than the 150 g maximum of the other printing.
Oil separating on top, same as every other documented version. It is the one thing nobody disagrees about.
Note the garnish unit here is tablespoons of crushed peanuts, where the magazine printing says teaspoons. Tablespoons is the sensible reading.
Two kilos of bone-in chicken means real bones — the collagen is what gives this soup its body, so skinless thighs alone will leave it thin.
commonMistakes: Treating this and the magazine version as the same recipe.
A tablespoon of extra-hot chilli powder without tasting first.
sources: Adapted from 'Dish of the Week: Zoe's Ghana Kitchen', melanmag.com, 23 January 2017. BYLINE AS PRINTED: 'Joy Joses' — that is the magazine's writer, NOT the recipe's author. The page credits the recipe to Zoe Adjonyoh / Zoe's Ghana Kitchen and carries the copyright line 'Zoe's Ghana Kitchen Ltd 2017'. Both credits are recorded: the dish is Adjonyoh's, the article is Joses's. No yield is stated. Quantities confirmed across two fetches (TWO-PASS).

Ingredients exactly as printed: 2kg mixed bone-in chicken pieces; 500-750ml water or good-quality chicken stock; 1 onion, finely diced; 5cm fresh root ginger, grated; 1 garlic clove, crushed; 8 green kpakpo shito chillies (or 1-2 Scotch Bonnet); 1 tablespoon extra-hot chilli powder; 1 tablespoon curry powder; 2 teaspoons sea salt; 1 teaspoon freshly ground black pepper; 500ml uncooked Chalé Sauce; 100–200g organic peanut butter; 1 red Scotch Bonnet chilli, pierced; 3 tablespoons crushed roasted peanuts (garnish); 2-3 spring onions, sliced julienne (garnish).
DONENESS CUES as printed: 'simmer 25 minutes until juices run clear'; then '45 minutes–1 hour... until peanut oil separates on top'.

THE DISAGREEMENT WITH THE SAME AUTHOR'S OTHER PRINTING, which is why both are published rather than merged. Chicken: 2 kg mixed bone-in here against 2 x 850 g skinned drumsticks and thighs at Sainsbury's Magazine (GHA013). Chalé sauce: 500 ml of ready-made uncooked sauce measured in here, against a fresh blend of listed ingredients there. Peanut butter: 100-200 g here, 100-150 g there. Chilli powder: 1 tablespoon extra-hot here, ½-1 teaspoon hot there. Chillies: 8 green kpakpo shito plus a pierced red scotch bonnet here, 1-2 scotch bonnets there. Stock: 500-750 ml here, 500 ml there. Garnish peanuts: 3 tablespoons here, 3 teaspoons there. NOT RECONCILED — these are two printings of one cook's soup and they differ in almost every quantity.

ON KPAKPO SHITO: the small round Ghanaian chilli, aromatic and moderately hot, and the one chilli most specific to Ghanaian cooking. The source itself offers scotch bonnet as the substitute, which is hotter and less fragrant.
For the full five-source peanut-quantity spread and the universal oil-separation endpoint, see the sources at GHA013; they are not repeated here.
The chalé sauce this recipe calls for is published separately at GHA031, where its own two printings also disagree.
healthBenefits: Bone-in chicken yields collagen and minerals a boneless cut does not.
Peanuts provide monounsaturated fat, niacin and vitamin E.
Kpakpo shito and scotch bonnet both supply capsaicin and vitamin C.
culturalNote: Having two printings of one cook's signature soup, differing in nearly every measurement, is a useful reminder that a recipe is a snapshot of a dish rather than its definition. The kpakpo shito in this version is the more Ghanaian choice — it is the chilli you actually find in Accra markets, and the scotch bonnet is the substitution offered to readers who cannot get it.
